method: The magic packet is built as six 0xFF bytes followed by the target MAC's six bytes repeated 16 times, which is 102 bytes, and an optional six-byte SecureOn password is appended to make 108 bytes. The MAC is read in any common notation - colon, dash, dotted Cisco or bare hex - after whitespace and the colon, dash and dot separators are removed, and must contain exactly 12 hex digits. The null address and the broadcast address are refused because no card can own them, and an address with the multicast bit set in its first byte is refused because a unicast NIC address always has an even first octet; a locally administered address has bit 1 set, is accepted, and is called out because virtual machines and randomised Wi-Fi addresses use one. A SecureOn password must be exactly 12 hex digits; an all-zero password is refused because it disables the feature and cannot be told apart from no password. The packet is emitted as lowercase hex with no separators, and the page also shows the six-byte sync prefix, the 96-byte MAC block and the optional six-byte tail separately. The destination is the limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255 on UDP port 9, which some equipment replaces with port 7; a browser cannot transmit raw UDP, so the hex is meant to be copied into a wake utility, a switch or router wake action, or a script. For the script case the page also generates three runnable senders from the same bytes - a POSIX shell script that pipes a printf-octal packet through socat, a Python 3 script using only the socket module, and a C99 program using POSIX sockets - with the MAC, the optional SecureOn tail and the 255.255.255.255:9 default baked in, each accepting an optional host and port, so the packet the page shows is the packet the file sends. Wake-on-LAN must be enabled in the card's firmware with standby power available, and the packet only reaches cards on the same Layer 2 segment. Everything runs in the browser without storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wake-on-LAN: the magic packet carries six 0xFF bytes, the target MAC repeated sixteen times (102 bytes) and an optional SecureOn password, and is sent to the limited broadcast address on UDP port 7 or 9.
wakeonlan(1): the magic packet consists of 6 times 0xFF followed by 16 times the hardware address, sent as a UDP datagram to 255.255.255.255 on port 9 by default.
